title: Invasion of coastal Maine by winter moth, Operophtera brumata (Lepidoptera: Geometridae)
content:
Abstract
Winter moth, Operophtera brumata L., is a geometrid defoliator from Europe that invaded Nova Scotia in the 1930s and the northeastern United States in the late 1990s. Between 2004 and 2011, it spread and caused widespread defoliation across eastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island but stopped its westward movement after that. In contrast, it has continued to spread northward along the coast of Maine. Here, we investigate the possible role of climate change in the distribution of winter moth in this region. We integrated aerial defoliation surveys conducted along the coast of Maine from 2017 to 2024 with pheromone trap surveys in Maine and the Maritime Provinces between 2021 and 2023 and identified collected moths as either being winter moth or the native Bruce spanworm, O. bruceata (Hulst) based on DNA analyses. We show a strong correlation between the proportion of winter moth at locations across Maine and the Maritime Provinces to the average minimum temperatures observed and mean number of days above freezing during the male flight period. Aerial surveys showed that, from 2017 to 2024, winter moth defoliation has moved steadily northward. We discuss how the changing distribution of winter moth may be caused by changes in winter temperatures along the Gulf of Maine and by inadvertent human movement of soil containing winter moth pupae from southern New England. All of the winter moths captured in Maine belonged to the lineage that originated in Massachusetts, whereas those from New Brunswick belonged to the lineage that originated in Nova Scotia.
